fiction: A story about a spelling season. The rivals are made up; the techniques are real.
status: DRAFT for the three-round review (BEE-CIRCUIT.md §12). Overrides: AMENDMENTS.md (10 Oct 2026).
authorNotes: cast.*.role, suspectBoard.portraits[].clearedBy, fairPlay, rounds[].deliver and every *Note / note field are author-facing. Never render them; they spoil the mystery.

Every key under rounds[].pieces is one on-screen line (≤ 60 words), read aloud by the device voice on a tap (amendment 3). pipWord, clue and beeFileFakeTip are small objects whose string fields are each one line.
On screen, cases are 'Surprise Stops'. No line says 'Case 1' etc.; the place or the night is named instead.
Placing never changes the outcome (L6): above/below letters differ, nothing else in a round depends on placing except rounds[8].pieces.suspense, which states both branches.
Clue cards ride the hall mail, so every V. clue reaches every path before the accusation even if a case is skipped (test 5). A case may repeat a clue on screen; the card is delivered once.
Puzzle items are the authored set and the demo set. In play the case runner may swap in same-pattern words at the child's band through pick(), keeping each item's rule.

signoffs.inv: — V. Abara, Pronouncer, for the Committee
signoffs.invNote: Drawn in an upright hand on every invitation. The accusation's look-again for the Pronouncer relies on it.

pixel.name: Pip
pixel.role: The rumour mill: one big word misused per note, the real meaning a tap away. The comic heart.

koi.name: Nova
koi.role: The steady friend; her nan's rule (say it twice). Corrects Dax's first fake tip. Team Night: Old English, younger lectern.

beaker.name: Rafi
beaker.tell: traces the letters on his palm
beaker.role: The palm trick; Kwame's study partner. Turns his back on Dax in Round V. Team Night: Latin, younger lectern.

panda.name: Suki
panda.role: Spells the unheard word in Round VII; Dax's rumour nearly strikes her round off (Case 4). Team Night: 'nobody's heard it', younger lectern.

comet.name: Dax
comet.role: The antagonist: fake tips, blame, one hidden bell, one rumour. A first warning, then a formal one. Reforms at the Finish Arch, clears Vesper in Case 5, captains Team Night from the bench.

astro.name: Mira
astro.tell: asks for the language of origin every time
astro.role: The Storm round. Corrects Dax's second fake tip. Team Night's Greek specialist (younger lectern).

scopey.name: Theo
scopey.tell: asks every question, every single word
scopey.role: The question tally (212, 640, 1,204, 1,977). Blamed for the misprints, cleared. His way saves the blackout final. Team Night: 'needs questions' (older lectern).

melody.name: Ines
melody.tell: mouths the word in French first
melody.role: Kwame's secret coach. Team Night's French specialist (older lectern).

samurai.name: Kwame
samurai.tell: hands behind his back, dead still
samurai.role: Two seasons without a public miss, until Round V. Comes back coached by Ines. The one who sits down next to Dax. Team Night: Latin and Greek (older lectern).

goldlegend.name: Vesper
goldlegend.role: Last year's champion and the silence. On the Suspect Board (a V. name, violet ink). The false solution in Case 5. Asks her first question in the blackout final; spells the Team Night tiebreaker.

pronouncer.name: V. Abara
pronouncer.role: The Pronouncer. Reads every word and writes every bee file, openly. Warm and plain-spoken; writes nothing secret to any child. On the Suspect Board only for his initial and his kindness: a red herring. Knows who V. is, as the whole Committee does, and promised not to say.

vale.name: Vale Penrallow
vale.tell: writes left-handed; always at the Pronouncer's elbow
vale.role: The Committee's runner: lays out the programmes, carries the sealed list envelopes, holds a bell-case key. Newest speller eight seasons ago, aged 8; placed last. She is V. The letters are a Committee tradition the Pronouncer approved; only her name is the children's mystery.

sage.name: Sage the Owl
sage.role: Host, the Library (the Grand Archive). Case 1 suspect: fell asleep at the press.

bolt.name: Bolt the Ram
bolt.role: Host, the Storm (the Eye of the Storm). Case 2 suspect: hid that the bell-case lock has been broken for a year.

hazel.name: Hazel the Hedgehog
hazel.tell: rolls into a ball under pressure
hazel.role: Host, the Roots (the Root Throne). Saw Kwame leave and told the Pronouncer at once (Case 3).

salty.name: Salty the Seal
salty.tell: applauds everything; every programme is damp

ratchet.name: Ratchet the Raccoon
ratchet.role: Host, the Junkyard (the Trickster's Gate). On the Suspect Board; cleared because every programme he writes has a misprint and V. never misspells.

dash.name: Dash the Hare
dash.role: Host, the Sprints (the Finish Arch). His spare key is the answer to Case 5.

duchess.name: Duchess the Cat
duchess.tell: sits on high shelves; regrets nothing
duchess.role: Host, the Big Stage (the Grand Marquee). Knocks the envelope off a shelf (Case 5).

sloane.name: Sloane
sloane.tell: never smiles, never asks a question twice
sloane.role: Ravenmere's captain. Everything is her speciality; a perfect record. Must lose for the first time, and doesn't know how. Season 2's antagonist camp.

ash.name: Ash Lindqvist
ash.tell: spells in step with a twin, one letter each
ash.role: Ravenmere. Memorised lists. Has never spelled apart from Aria.

aria.name: Aria Lindqvist
aria.tell: spells in step with a twin, one letter each
aria.role: Ravenmere. Memorised lists. Has never spelled apart from Ash.

arjun.name: Arjun
arjun.tell: names the origin before the pronouncer finishes
arjun.role: Ravenmere. Origins of every kind. Respects the Circuit and won't say so.

mei.name: Mei
mei.tell: writes every word in the air first
mei.role: Ravenmere's youngest. Slips the child a note in pencil after Team Night; a Season 2 seed for V.'s second hand.

portraits.clearedBy: Round VI letter ('Not me. I don't write notes.'); Round IX letter (the violet pen was a gift).

rounds.technique: Wait for the whole word, then say it back before your first letter.
rounds.lesson: The Champion's Routine — say, spell, say
rounds.vWhere: on your chair, before the post came

pieces.inv: Welcome to the Bee Circuit. Nine rounds. One season. The Grand Marquee at the end. Seated in chairs two and three: Pip, who starts before the word is finished, and Nova, who says every word twice. One more thing: a Circuit tradition, letters signed V. The Committee knows who writes them. Working out who is up to you.
pieces.prog: Please do not feed the bees. The bees are competing. — Barnaby
pieces.drama: Pip blurts his first word before the Pronouncer has finished it. Round one forgives, so he stays standing. In round two he does it again, and sits down. Then he cheers louder than anyone for every speller left.
pieces.laugh: The Pronouncer: 'Say it back for me.' Pip: 'Say it back for me.' The Pronouncer: 'Not the instructions, Pip.' At his elbow, the Committee's runner doesn't even blink.
pieces.suspense: Before the doors open, the Committee's runner lays a programme on every chair. At the end of the row sits one chair with a card that reads RESERVED. Nobody sits in it.
pieces.above: You waited. I saw. My nan's rule: say it twice. Once to hear it, once to check you heard it. — Nova
pieces.below: So close. Say it back before your first letter, like the Pronouncer asks. My nan's rule: say it twice. — Nova
pieces.v: Say it back. The chair at the end of the row is waiting for someone. So are you. — V.
pieces.dax: A postcard from a venue you haven't reached: 'Heard you got through the Meadow. The Sprints are mine. — D. (fastest in round one, ask anyone)'
pieces.pip: Dax is ubiquitous, which means very quick. (You-be-quick. It's right there in the word.) — Pip

pipWord.real: seeming to be everywhere at once

pieces.cliff: The postcard's stamp is from the Finish Arch, in the eighth region. You've only finished the first. How is he already there?

clue.text: Note 1 was on your chair before the post came. It quotes the Pronouncer: 'Say it back.'

rounds.technique: Ask before you spell: the definition, a sentence, the part of speech, the origin, other pronunciations. The Pronouncer has to answer.
rounds.lesson: Ask the Right Questions — be a word detective

pieces.inv: The Grand Archive requests silence, which Theo will not provide. You may ask the Pronouncer for a definition, a sentence, the part of speech. He has to answer.
pieces.prog: We admire Theo's curiosity. We have ordered more chairs. Our press is run by a typesetter who learned English from a parrot. — Sage
pieces.drama: Theo asks eleven questions about one word and spells it perfectly. The speller two seats down falls asleep.
pieces.laugh: The Pronouncer, for the eleventh time: 'Yes, Theo. It is still a noun.' The runner refills his water glass without being asked.
pieces.suspense: By the Archive door hangs a programme from every season, framed. Eight seasons back, one line: 'Newest speller: Vale Penrallow, aged 8, placed last.'
pieces.above: You asked three questions and beat me. Imagine eleven. They have to answer. Questions asked this season: 212. — Theo
pieces.below: You asked one question. Ask five: definition, sentence, part of speech, origin, alternate pronunciation. Questions asked this season: 212. — Theo
pieces.v: You guess instead of asking. Tonight the list will lie to you. Read it twice. — V.
pieces.dax: In the corridor, a 'tip': 'Separate has an e in the middle, everyone knows.' Nova, passing, says it twice, loud: 'Sep-a-rate. Sep-a-rate.' Three spellers fix their notes. Dax shrugs.

beeFileFakeTip.tip: Separate has an e in the middle: seperate.
beeFileFakeTip.truth: S-E-P-A-R-A-T-E. The middle is an a: there's a rat in separate. It comes from Latin separare, from se- (apart) and parare (to make ready).

pieces.pip: Theo is loquacious, which is a kind of lizard. — Pip
pieces.cliff: Surprise Stop 1: URGENT. 'The list for the Colosseum is back from the press. Every word is wrong.' V. predicted it.

clue.text: A framed programme, eight seasons old: 'Newest speller: Vale Penrallow, aged 8, placed last.' Another V.

rounds.technique: Take the Latin apart: prefix, root, ending. Split it before you spell it.

pieces.inv: Latin prefixes today. The Colosseum seats thousands; today it seats us. In chair four: Rafi, who takes every root apart before he writes a letter.
pieces.prog: This programme is late. All of my programmes are late. — Tullia
pieces.drama: Rafi traces every word on his palm and lasts deep into the round. By the end his hand is shaking. He keeps tracing.
pieces.laugh: Tullia's programme arrives after the round has finished. The runner hands it out anyway, straight-faced, one per chair.
pieces.suspense: A violet pen has been left on your chair. Violet is Vesper's ink.
pieces.above: You beat me on circumference. Circum means around; fer means carry. The line carried around. Split it before you spell it. Draw the next word small on your palm. — Rafi
pieces.below: Circum means around, fer means carry: circumference is the line carried around. Split it first, then spell it. Try my palm trick. — Rafi
pieces.v: Every long word is a short word wearing a coat. When the bell goes missing, look for the one who's scared of thunder. — V.
pieces.dax: The night the list lied, Dax told everyone Theo did it: 'Who else hangs round a printing press?' Cleared, Theo asks him in front of the whole Archive: 'What made you think it was me?' His 640th question this season. Dax has no answer. He shrugs it off.
pieces.pip: Rafi is meticulous, which is a type of fish. — Pip

pipWord.real: very careful about every small detail

pieces.cliff: The Storm invitation says Vesper is 'already qualified for the Grand Marquee'. The RESERVED chair now has a name.

clue.text: The night the list lied, the runner fixed the last line by hand: left hand, slanting left, like every V. note. The Pronouncer signed under it, straight up. And on your chair, a violet pen. Vesper writes in violet.

rounds.technique: Ask for the origin. In words from Greek, an f sound is often spelled ph, a k sound often ch, and an i sound often y.
rounds.vWhere: on your chair, before the post came

pieces.inv: Today's weather: Greek, with a strong chance of ph. Seated in chair one: Mira, who asks every word where it was born.
pieces.prog: Expect thunder, and a ringing in your ears. — Bolt
pieces.drama: Thunder hits mid-word. Mira doesn't flinch. She asks the origin, hears 'Greek', and smiles.
pieces.laugh: Mira asks for the origin of the word 'the'. The Pronouncer answers, at length, delighted.
pieces.suspense: That night, before Kwame's round, the Committee bell vanishes from its locked glass case. V. called it a round ago. Surprise Stop 2: URGENT.
pieces.above: You asked for the origin twice. Do it every time. Greek words travel with their luggage: ph, ch, y. — Mira
pieces.below: Phantom with an f! Ask where it came from and the word tells you its rules. — Mira
pieces.v: Words keep their passports. Check them. Someone in this hall is about to lose more than a round. — V.
pieces.dax: In the corridor: 'Rhythm's got an i in it, everyone knows.' Mira, without looking up: 'Greek. Y.' Two spellers who were listening stop listening to him.

beeFileFakeTip.tip: Rhythm has an i in it: rhithm.
beeFileFakeTip.truth: R-H-Y-T-H-M. It comes from Greek rhythmos, and the Greek letter upsilon comes into English as y. There is no i anywhere in it.

pieces.pip: Mira is clairvoyant, which means she always clears up after herself. — Pip

pipWord.real: claiming to see the future, or things beyond the ordinary senses

pieces.cliff: V. said someone would lose more than a round. Who?

clue.text: V. always knows your weak spot. So does the bee file, the Pronouncer's scouting report. He writes it. The runner carries it.

rounds.technique: Build the word from its parts: prefix, root, suffix. Never skip one.
rounds.vWhere: on the steps of the Root Throne
rounds.orderNote: The laugh eases the hall before the crack, never after it.

pieces.inv: Kwame has not misspelled a word in public in two seasons. Seated beside him: you. Dax spells today on a first warning from the Committee.
pieces.prog: Spectators are asked not to roll up into balls during sudden death. — Hazel
pieces.drama: Kwame's word is reconnaissance. He leaves out an s. The hall goes silent. Hands still behind his back, he walks out. The runner holds the door for him and says nothing.
pieces.laugh: Hazel rolls into a ball during sudden death. The hall laughs, for the last time today.
pieces.suspense: The hall stays quiet long after the door shuts. A round ago, V. wrote that someone would lose more than a round.
pieces.above: Now you know my weakness. French. Build every word from parts and you'll never crack like I did. I'm going to the Far Shore to fix mine. — K.
pieces.below: You built it from parts and nearly had me. Prefix, root, suffix: never skip one. I have a weakness now. French. I'm going to the Far Shore to fix it. — K.
pieces.v: Parts first, then the whole. You skip the suffix. And when a strong one breaks, the loud one gets louder. Watch. — V.
pieces.dax: Kwame is already out of the building when Dax says it, loud, in the corridor: 'Told you. Nobody's perfect. Two seasons, gone in one word.' Nobody laughs. Rafi turns his back on him.
pieces.pip: Kwame is imperturbable, which means he can't be turned into a turnip. — Pip

pipWord.misuse: can't be turned into a turnip
pipWord.real: calm; impossible to upset or fluster

pieces.cliff: Kwame's room is empty, his bag still on the bed. The Pronouncer says he's safe, and that's all he'll say. Surprise Stop 3: URGENT.

clue.text: A V. note turned up inside the locked bell case. Two keys open it: one on the Committee's ring, one on the runner's lanyard. Unless Bolt is right that the lock has been broken for a year. Then anyone could.

rounds.technique: Loanwords keep their home spelling. Ask the language, then listen for the letters it hides, often at the end.

pieces.inv: Fog on the Far Shore. Today's words came ashore from elsewhere. Seated: Ines, who mouths every word in French first, and Kwame, who has come back.
pieces.drama: Ines faces Kwame, the speller she has secretly coached, in the last rounds. She tells the Pronouncer it's the hardest she has ever had to spell against anyone.
pieces.laugh: Salty applauds every word, including the wrong ones.
pieces.suspense: Vesper's letter, one line: 'Not me. I don't write notes. — Vesper.'
pieces.above: Écoute la fin. Listen to the ending. French hides its letters at the end. You heard them today. — Ines
pieces.below: Écoute la fin. Ballet ends in a t you never hear. The quiet letters beat you. — Ines
pieces.v: The silent letters are the loudest. Next round, a word none of you has heard. Its parts have. — V.
pieces.dax: Dax sits alone on the dock. Nobody sits with him. He is writing something.
pieces.pip: Ines is bilingual, which means she has two lungs. — Pip

pipWord.real: able to speak two languages well

pieces.cliff: In the Junkyard invitation, Dax is listed eighth on the Circuit table, right behind Suki.

clue.text: Vesper's letter: 'Not me. I don't write notes.' Is it true?

rounds.technique: Nerve. Facing a word you've never heard: breathe out, ask everything, and spell what its parts say.
rounds.vWhere: on your chair, in the slanting hand

pieces.inv: The Trickster's Gate round includes one word no speller here has heard before. Seated: Suki, whom the lights do nothing to.
pieces.prog: Three chairs have been borowed and will be returned evenchually. — Ratchet
pieces.progNote: Deliberate misprints (borrowed, eventually). Ratchet's programmes always have one; the Suspect Board uses it to clear him.
pieces.drama: The unheard word comes to Suki first, and for the first time ever she freezes. She breathes out, asks all five questions, and spells it right.
pieces.laugh: Ratchet tries to 'borrow' the Pronouncer's microphone mid-round. The runner takes it back without a word. 'Thank you, Vale,' says the Pronouncer.
pieces.suspense: By evening the rumour is everywhere: the word is fake, and Suki's round should be struck. Surprise Stop 4.
pieces.above: The lights do something to everyone. I breathe out first. Out, not in. You did it today. — Suki
pieces.below: You held your breath on the hard one. Breathe out. Then ask everything. — Suki
pieces.v: Breathe out before the hard ones, not after. And the rumour has one author. He is fast. — V.
pieces.dax: Dax is out of the hall before Suki's last letter, talking fast in the corridor. By evening everyone has heard the rumour. Nobody can say who said it first.
pieces.pip: Suki is nonchalant, which is a kind of soup. — Pip

pipWord.real: calm and relaxed; seeming not to worry

pieces.cliff: The Finish Arch invitation: Dax's own round. He hasn't sent a postcard.

clue.text: V. knew about the unheard word a round before the Committee announced it. The list is sealed in front of two people: the Pronouncer, and the runner who carries it. Her name is Vale. She's sixteen.

rounds.technique: Pace. Fast early is not fast late: keep the steady beat, one syllable at a time, as calm in the last round as in the first.
rounds.vWhere: under the Finish Arch, while it was taped off

pieces.inv: A speed round. The Committee notes that one speller has received a formal warning and will spell under observation.
pieces.prog: The round will start at the bell. — Dash
pieces.drama: Dax flies through round one, then fades, rocking on his heels, exactly as his tell says. After the last word, the screen cuts straight to the result card.
pieces.laugh: Dash lets himself into the bell room with his own spare key and rings the bell four minutes early. The round starts anyway.
pieces.suspense: The Finish Arch is taped off all morning. At the bell, the runner takes the tape down. Underneath lies a folded card with your name on it, in the slanting hand.
pieces.above: You went slow on purpose and beat me. I'm sorry about the fake tips. And Theo. And the bell. And Suki. Mostly Suki. — D.
pieces.below: I finished ahead of you today, and it doesn't feel like winning. I'm sorry about the fake tips. And Theo. And the bell. And Suki. Mostly Suki. — D.
pieces.v: Steady beat wins late. Not everyone who writes to you wants to beat you. — V.
pieces.dax: His home hall: he sent you that first postcard from here. Under observation, he doesn't whisper a single tip. He doesn't talk to anyone at all.
pieces.pip: Dax is contrite, which means he can't be trusted with a kite. (I looked it up after. It means sorry. He is.) — Pip

pipWord.misuse: can't be trusted with a kite
pipWord.real: truly sorry for something you did wrong

pieces.cliff: The Grand Marquee invitation, on gold card: 'Seated in chair one: Vesper.' And on the back, in the slanting hand: 'The envelope will open before anyone opens it. — V.'

clue.text: Dax had V. notes too: a whole stack, all season, every one ignored. He thought you were writing them.

rounds.technique: Everything at once: wait, ask, find the origin, take it apart, breathe out, keep the beat.
rounds.accusation: see top-level accusation (opens after this round's mail)

pieces.inv: The final. Every speller you have met will be in the hall. Seated in chair one: Vesper, defending champion. Curtain up at seven.
pieces.drama: Halfway through, the Grand Marquee's lights go out. The round goes on by voice alone, and Theo's way becomes everyone's way: ask first, spell second. Then Vesper, who has never asked for anything, speaks into the dark: 'Language of origin, please.' The hall goes silent.
pieces.laugh: Pip, in the dark: 'Good. Now nobody can see me start early.'
pieces.suspense: The championship word arrives in a sealed envelope, carried in by the runner. Finish above Vesper and it's yours to spell; finish below and it's hers. Either way, the card shows the word, its origin and the technique that cracks it.
pieces.above: You beat me by asking. I stopped asking the year I won, because it felt weak. Watching you ask everything was annoying. Then useful. The violet pen was mine. Keep it. — Vesper
pieces.below: I won because I asked, the first time in a year. You asked everything all season. Annoying. Then useful. The violet pen was mine. You were writing in pencil; it was painful to watch. Keep it. — Vesper
pieces.v: You asked everything tonight. Ask one more: who was there every single round? — V.
pieces.dax: In the dark, Dax stops rocking on his heels. 'Could I have the definition, please?' Theo, somewhere to his left: 'Your first. I'm on 1,977.'
pieces.pip: Vesper is formidable. I looked it up. It means what it sounds like. — Pip

pipWord.real: so strong or skilled that you have to respect it

pieces.cliff: A navy envelope with a silver crest: 'Ravenmere Academy challenges the Bee Circuit to a Team Bee. Tomorrow night. Your hall. Do try to keep up. — Sloane, Captain.'

clue.text: The night before the final, backstage, the Pronouncer said it plainly: 'I know who V. is. So does the whole Committee. I promised not to say. It isn't mine to tell.'

turn.scene: Dax sits alone at the arrival desk under the Arch. Kwame walks over and sits down beside him.

line.true: Dax, without looking up: 'You came over. Both of you. Nobody's come over all season.'
line.false: A minute later you join them. Dax, without looking up: 'Thanks for the minute. I needed it.'

choice.note: Both lead to the same scene. This is the only line the choice changes. Flavour only, never the outcome.

turn.kwame: I crack too. Two seasons, gone in one word. You said it. You were right. Welcome.
turn.dax: I go fast because slow scares me. Slow is where you find out you don't know it.
turn.notesIntro: Then he takes a stack of cards from his pocket. V. notes, sent to him, all season. Every one ignored.
notes: Round one is not the whole bee. — V.
Ask one question. Just one. — V.
Fast is a start, not a finish. — V.
turn.daxOnNotes: I thought YOU were writing them.

apologies.text: I said you wrecked the list. You didn't. I said it because you were easy to say it about. Sorry. — D.
apologies.reply: Accepted. One question: why me? (That's 1,204.) — Theo

apologies.text: The rumour was mine. You were one place ahead of me, and I wanted that place more than I wanted to be fair. Sorry. — D.
apologies.reply: Breathe out, Dax. Out, not in. — Suki

apologies.text: What I said in the corridor. And 'not my problem.' Both wrong. Sorry. — D.
apologies.reply: You were right about one thing. Nobody's perfect. That's what a team is for. — K.

turn.toTheChild: In rounds[7].pieces.above / below: the fake tips, Theo, the bell, Suki.

cases.title: The Misprinted List
cases.theme: The Library, 'every rule English wrote down': proofreading by the rules.
cases.clock: The Colosseum round is at 9:00, and the Pronouncer reads from paper.
cases.impossible: Every word on the only list is misspelled. The press was locked, and the printer swears he checked.

suspects.secret: He needs glasses and hasn't told anyone.
He was at the press eleven times, 'only checking definitions'. He can't sleep the night before a round.

cases.falseSolution: Theo tampered with it. Dax says so first, and loudest.
planted: Round II programme (Sage): 'Our press is run by a typesetter who learned English from a parrot.'
Round II V. note: 'Tonight the list will lie to you. Read it twice.'
cases.escalation: 11:40 p.m. The backup list turns up. It's misprinted too, in exactly the same places.

puzzle.brief: Twelve words from the list. Find each misprint and fix it. One of them isn't wrong at all, and spotting that is the key.
puzzle.rule: Every misprint is a word missing a letter you can't hear.

items.why: Not a misprint. American spelling dropped the u on purpose; British spelling kept it. Both are right.

choices: The typesetter worked from a parrot's dictation, and every letter you can't hear went missing.
The printer misprinted it on purpose.

reveal: The apprentice set the type from the parrot's dictation. A parrot can only say what it hears, so every letter you can't hear went missing.
The backup was copied from the first list. Same holes, same places.
And color? The parrot dropped a u nobody says, and American dictionaries dropped it too, on purpose. Colour and color are both right.
Theo is cleared. The printer gets glasses. Sage is forgiven.
The runner, who carries the lists, fixes the last line by hand. Left hand. Her writing slants left. The Pronouncer signs underneath, straight up.
Dax shrugs: 'Could've been Theo.'
cases.clueOnScreen: v-slant (delivered as Round III's clue card on every path)
cases.lastChill: On the press, a V. note: 'Read it twice. Then look at who blamed whom. — V.'

cases.title: The Bell That Went Missing
cases.theme: The Storm, 'Greek blows in like weather': a Greek clue trail.
cases.clock: Kwame's round starts in 30 minutes. No bell, no bee.
cases.impossible: The bell vanished from a locked glass case, and the glass is unbroken.

suspects.secret: He's scared of storms, and hides it.
The lock has been broken for a year, and he never reported it.
He shouts 'sabotage!' first. He hasn't practised, and wants the round delayed.

cases.falseSolution: A saboteur stole the bell to cancel the round.
planted: Round IV programme (Bolt): 'Expect thunder, and a ringing in your ears.'

visitorsNote: Stop Visitors (§10, amendment 4). Framed historically: who they were to the ancient Greeks, Romans or Norse, or a dated line for a real person, and how the word reached English. Respectful voice (Bizzing India docs/05 §1–§2): no comedy, no speaking role, never 'myth' as a synonym for 'false', uncertainty stated plainly. Norse and classical religion have practitioners today; cards speak historically and never call the gods false. None of these appears in the story (D9). A visitor shows only where the build script finds its word on that stop's own list (eponyms.json); stop stays null until then. Every card goes through the three-round review.

visitors.card: To the ancient Greeks, Atlas was a Titan who held up the sky. In 1595 a book of maps by Gerardus Mercator came out under the title Atlas, and the word came to mean any book of maps.

sources.ref: Hesiod, Theogony (Atlas holds up the sky)
Gerardus Mercator, Atlas sive Cosmographicae Meditationes (Duisburg, 1595)

visitors.card: To the ancient Greeks, Hermes was the messenger of the gods. Much later, books of alchemy were credited to a legendary 'Thrice-Great Hermes', said to have made a seal that let no air through. Hermetic came to mean sealed tight.
To the ancient Greeks, Iris was the goddess of the rainbow and a messenger of the gods. Her name is the Greek word for rainbow. Iridescent means shimmering with rainbow colours, like a soap bubble.

In Greek stories, later retold by the Roman poet Ovid, Echo was a mountain nymph who could only repeat the last words she heard. Her name is the Greek word for a sound that comes back, and English kept it: echo.

To the ancient Greeks, Pan was the god of shepherds and wild places, with a goat's legs and horns. Sudden, causeless fear in lonely places was blamed on him. The Greek word panikos, 'of Pan', reached English as panic.

In Greek myth, Tantalus was a king punished in the underworld: the water around him drained away when he bent to drink, and the fruit above him rose out of reach. To tantalise is to keep what someone wants just out of reach.

To the ancient Greeks, Hypnos was the god of sleep. In 1843 the Scottish surgeon James Braid named hypnotism after him, believing it was a kind of sleep. It isn't, but the name stuck, and hypnosis followed.

In a story told by the Roman writer Apuleius, Psyche was a mortal princess who won the love of Cupid and was made immortal. Her name is the Greek word for the soul or mind. Psychology, the study of the mind, is built on it.
To the ancient Greeks, the Titans were the giant elder gods who ruled before Zeus and the Olympians. Titanic means as huge and powerful as a Titan.

To the ancient Romans, Janus was the god of doorways and beginnings, shown with two faces, one looking back and one looking ahead. The Romans named a month for him, Ianuarius, and English made it January, the doorway of our year.
To the ancient Romans, Mars was the god of war, and the month of March was his. Martial, meaning to do with fighting, as in martial arts, comes from his name.

To the ancient Romans, Juno was queen of the gods and protector of women and marriage. June may be named after her, but even the Romans weren't sure: in his poem about the calendar, Ovid lets three goddesses argue over the month and never gives a verdict.

sources.ref: Ovid, Fasti, Book 6 (Juno, Juventas and Concordia each claim June)

visitors.card: To the ancient Romans, Vulcan was the god of fire and the forge. Italian named burning mountains after him, vulcano, and English borrowed the word: volcano.
To the ancient Romans, Ceres was the goddess of grain and the harvest. The Latin cerealis meant 'of Ceres', and English took it for grain crops, and for the grains in a breakfast bowl: cereal.
To the ancient Romans, Fortuna was the goddess of luck, good and bad. Her name is the Latin word fortuna, chance, and it reached English as fortune.
To the ancient Romans, Mercury was the quick-footed messenger of the gods. A planet and a quick, shining liquid metal took his name, and mercurial came to mean quick and changeable.
To the Anglo-Saxons he was Tiw, and to the Norse Týr: a god of war. When Germanic peoples took over the Roman week, the day of Mars, the Roman war god, became Tiw's day: Tuesday.
To the Anglo-Saxons he was Woden, and to the Norse Odin: chief of the gods and a seeker of wisdom. The Roman day of Mercury became Woden's day: Wednesday, with a d you never hear.
To the Norse, Thor was the god of thunder, who carried a hammer. The Anglo-Saxons called him Thunor, which is also their word for thunder. The Roman day of Jupiter became Thor's day: Thursday.

To the Norse, Frigg was queen of the gods and wife of Odin; the Anglo-Saxons called her Frige. The Roman day of Venus became her day: Friday. Some scholars think the goddess Freyja fits Venus better, and they still argue about it.

John Montagu, 4th Earl of Sandwich (1718–1792), an English politician. By 1762 people were eating 'a sandwich', named after him. The story goes that he wanted a meal he could eat without leaving the table, but historians say nobody can prove it.

sources.ref: Edward Gibbon, journal entry, 24 November 1762 ('a bit of cold meat, or a Sandwich')
Pierre-Jean Grosley, Londres (1770), recounting a 1765 visit
N. A. M. Rodger, The Insatiable Earl (1993)

visitors.card: Adolphe Sax (1814–1894), a Belgian instrument maker. In 1846 he patented a new instrument: a metal body, played with a reed. It took his name and the Greek word phone, voice or sound: the saxophone.

James Brudenell, 7th Earl of Cardigan (1797–1868), a British army officer. By the 1860s a knitted wool jacket that buttons down the front carried his name. He didn't invent it, and why it took his name is not certain.

Rudolf Diesel (1858–1913), a German engineer. In the 1890s he designed an engine that squeezes air until it is hot enough to light the fuel without a spark. The engine, and the fuel it burns, carry his name: diesel.

Isaac Newton (1643–1727), an English mathematician and scientist who set out the laws of motion and of gravity. In 1948 an international conference on measurement named the unit of force after him: the newton.
visitors.datesNote: New Style dates; by the calendar England then used, he was born on 25 December 1642.

visitors.card: Marie Curie (1867–1934) and Pierre Curie (1859–1906), scientists in Paris who studied radioactivity. In 1910, at a congress in Brussels, scientists named a unit of radioactivity the curie, in honour of Pierre, and many took it to honour Marie too.
